articles.title: Google Explains How To Use HTML Sitemaps For SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Google’s John Mueller and Martin Splitt recently discussed how HTML sitemaps may still be useful for SEO even though the XML standard has largely replaced it.

Before the introduction of XML sitemaps, SEOs and site owners typically added internal and external links to new web pages to ensure that they got crawled and started ranking.

They also added a link from the footer of the home page (or every page) to an HTML sitemap where a gigantic list of links to inner pages could be crawled and aid in getting those pages indexed. Most SEOs populated the HTML sitemap with every page on their site that was considered useful to rank. Other pages, like the About Us pages, were left off of the HTML sitemap.

It’s possible that Google was already using RSS feeds well before the introduction of XML sitemaps. For example, a 2004 university research paper documented that RSS feeds could be used by web crawlers to identify new and recently modified web pages and reduce crawling bandwidth by up to 40%.

But because RSS feeds weren’t universally implemented, they were likely impractical to use for crawl discovery. That’s probably why GYM (Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft) joined forces to agree on a single XML sitemap standard that is used to this day.

HTML Sitemaps Not A Replacement For XML Sitemaps

During the course of their recent Search Off The Record episode, Martin Splitt asked if SEOs and site owners were locked into using XML sitemaps OR if it was okay to use HTML sitemaps.

Google’s Mueller explained that HTML sitemaps are not a replacement for XML sitemaps because they lack the structural features inherent in XML sitemaps.

“Ah yes, HTML sitemaps. That I think is very confusing to the average person because you probably know what XML is and what HTML is, but a lot of people when they open an XML file, they see those weird brackets and they’re like, oh, this is HTML or very similar, right?

It looks like this weird programming stuff. And they’re called the same, but an HTML sitemap is basically almost like a map of your website for users. It’s not something that replaces an XML sitemap file.

Of course, if someone is crawling your website and they find an HTML sitemap file, they can crawl those links like any other link on a website, so that’s helpful.

But it’s not the case that the HTML sitemap can be submitted as a sitemap file. It can’t be processed one-to-one the same way as an XML sitemap file because it doesn’t have this strict structure to it. It’s basically a collection of links.”

Somewhat surprisingly, Google’s Mueller explained that HTML sitemaps can still be used. His answer implied deploying them as a part of a navigational system for users. Mueller used the example of an ecommerce site, but his answer can apply to any kind of website.

In his example, an HTML sitemap enables site visitors to easily reach the top-level product (or topic) category pages from which site visitors can drill down to a product (or topic) they are interested in.

His answer was in response to Martin Splitt’s question:

“But that still would help crawling because from this place we can find all the links as well. It’s just not as structured and clear cut as an XML sitemap, I guess.”

“Yes, absolutely. And it’s something I think that a lot of HTML sitemaps, they don’t include everything.

So if you have an e-commerce site, you wouldn’t list all of your products in an HTML sitemap file. You would list maybe the categories so that people can go to the right place, but then pick out the product individually. So it’s similar, but not exactly the same.”

For some readers, this is a relatively new idea. For others, the concept of an HTML sitemap might be perceived as old and outdated like directory links or reciprocal link arrangements. And yet, Google’s John Mueller says that they can be useful for users, which means HTML sitemaps could be useful for Google.

If you’re going to do it, do it in a way that’s useful for users, and you may find that site visitors will start using and recommending more pages from the site, and Google will pick up on those signals.

HTML sitemaps have a long history in SEO. Before XML sitemaps, they helped search engines discover pages and were used to distribute PageRank.

HTML sitemaps are not replacements for XML sitemaps. Google explains that they serve different purposes, although both can support crawling.

Google confirms HTML sitemaps are still useful. They can improve website navigation for users while helping search engines discover pages.

HTML sitemaps don’t need to contain every page. Google suggests organizing them around useful navigation paths rather than creating enormous collections of links.

The SEO value of HTML sitemaps starts with users. Making websites easier to navigate can also benefit crawling and content discovery.

articles.title: 8 best link-in-bio tools for brands and creators in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Between character count limitations and linking restrictions, one clickable URL in your bio could fix a lot of problems.

Link-in-bio tools let you centralize your social links with a dynamic landing page that hosts all the URLs for your social posts. That means a single link will lead to many destinations. You just need to update the landing page with the destination URL for every new post you share on your socials.

Your bio link stays the same, but people still get to visit the intended destination for your latest posts.

So link-in-bio tools for Instagram are especially useful for bypassing the platform’s restrictions against clickable links in the caption. This leads to real traffic that you could otherwise lose without a clickable URL to lead visitors to the right destination. And traffic could ultimately turn into conversions.

In this post, we rank the best link-in-bio tools to back up your social media efforts. Let’s dive in.

1. Sprout Social

Best for: Social teams that need link-in-bio features baked into a larger social media workflow

SproutLink is a built-in link-in-bio tool that comes with your Sprout Social plan. It lets you build a custom landing page featuring a clickable, shoppable grid that mirrors your Instagram. So when people click on your bio link, it’s easier to pick up where they left off on the platform.

You can create a custom branded URL that adds credibility to your link, giving audiences the confidence to click through. Sprout’s analysis even found that our link-in-bio Instagram tool led to a 17% average lift in profile engagement per day for customers using SproutLink.

The feature integrates with the rest of your Instagram publishing workflow, which means you get to add the destination links as you create and schedule new posts. And the clickable posts will automatically appear in your custom landing page.

This saves you the trouble of using a dedicated tool to add and manage your links separately from your publishing ecosystem.

Key features:

  • Custom branded URL
  • Visual grid-style landing page
  • Hourly-updated link analytics
  • Link scheduling
  • Branding and customization

Pros:

  • Seamless integration with social media management workflows
  • Robust analytics insights into page views and per-post click counts

Source: Sprout Social

2. Linktree

Best for: Solopreneurs and individual creators needing a tool with fast, no-frills setup

Linktree is a straightforward tool often touted as the “original” in the link-in-bio category. You can choose from pre-built designs to create a landing page that hosts all your links in one place.

The tool connects your content across different social networks, not just Instagram. You can even use QR codes to send offline traffic to your Linktree page.

The free tier lets you manage an unlimited number of basic links and comes with limited analytics. Upgrading to a paid plan unlocks deeper analytics and customization tools.

Key features:

  • Multi-platform link management
  • Supports unlimited links
  • QR codes for offline traffic
  • Traffic monetization support
  • Basic publishing and scheduling tools

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • Easy, beginner-friendly setup

Cons:

  • Branding and customization require paid upgrades
  • Bare-bones analytics with the free plan

Source: Linktree

3. Beacons

Best for: Creators needing a tool to monetize their social media links

Beacons is an all-in-one creator platform with a built-in link-in-bio tool. It functions as a creator-commerce suite rather than a simple link page. So in addition to managing your URLs, you get to build a unified business hub featuring images, music, products and signup forms.

The free plan comes with basic analytics and a customizable link in bio. Custom domains and advanced marketing features require a paid upgrade.

Key features:

  • Built-in storefront
  • Multimedia embedding
  • Email capture, media kits, tipping
  • Digital products and affiliate links
  • Auto-updating media kits
  • Basic link analytics

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • Robust monetization features

Cons:

  • Functions separately from your publishing workflow
  • 9% seller fees with the free plan

Source: Beacons

4. Milkshake

Best for: Beginners needing a fast, visual, mobile-first builder

Milkshake positions itself as a “website builder” rather than a link-in-bio tool. You can build a custom website by putting together multiple “Cards” (or pages) that each serves a specific purpose. The Links Card lets you stack multiple URLs that lead to different destinations, functioning as a link-in-bio page.

The template-driven, mobile-native design mimics a mini app rather than a scrolling link list. This makes it ideal for beginners who need to quickly put together a custom page for their links.

The free version of the tool comes with up to 30 days of analytics data and basic customization.

Key features:

  • App-based website builder
  • Supports unlimited links
  • QR codes for offline traffic
  • Link analytics
  • Monetization tools

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • Fast and easy to use for beginners

Cons:

  • Functions separately from your publishing workflow
  • 12% seller fees with the free plan

articles.title: Ticker: Former WH Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt Joins Fox News
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Top of the Ticker: The Fox News-to-White House pipeline has changed direction. The network announced Monday that former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is joining as a contributor.

Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott announced the move. Leavitt will begin her role on Sunday, November 1, providing political analysis and commentary across all platforms.

“I am grateful for the opportunity to continue appearing on Fox News Channel as an official member of the extraordinary team at Fox News Media,” said Leavitt.

Her tenure as the White House Press Secretary ran from January 2025 to August 2026, making her the 36th person to hold the role and the only one so far during President Donald Trump ’s second term.

Meanwhile, Fox News Media’s streaming service, Fox Nation, is gearing up for Halloween by premiering a three-part series about the magician Harry Houdini . Dropping on Wednesday, October 14, Houdini: Back from the Dead marks new ground-breaking territory for the streaming platform, as it’s the first full-length project to use entirely AI-generated imagery to bring Houdini to life, with the 100th anniversary of his passing approaching.

“We’re proud to showcase a new form of historical storytelling that allows viewers to experience Houdini’s remarkable life in his own words, while remaining rooted in extensive research and historical accuracy,” said Lauren Petterson , president of Fox Nation.

Programming plans : Before CBS News’ official election night broadcast on Tuesday, November 3, the news outlet is launching a new digital show focusing on election data. The Nerd Show, hosted by CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto alongside congressional correspondent Caitlin Huey-Burns , will begin at 5 p.m. ET streaming on YouTube, X, and CBS News’ owned and operated digital channels, including its streaming network, CBS News 24/7.

If you can’t beat them : ABC News is the latest news organization to introduce vertical video as part of its app offerings. Verts, as the format is known across the Disney universe, will feature an interactive feed of fast, factual news sourced from ABC News’ linear, streaming, and ABC Owned television programming, along with original content from ABC News anchors, correspondents, analysts, and featured voices.

Budding author : MS NOW anchor and senior business analyst Stephanie Ruhle will debut her latest book, The New Rules: Work, Life, Money and the Power of Minding Your Own Business, on March 2, 2027. Published by Avid Reader Press, a division of Simon & Schuster, Ruhle’s book offers powerful, candid, counterintuitive lessons on work, life, money, and relationships.

Milestones : Two major cable news programs recently marked their 15th anniversary. CNN’s Erin Burnett OutFront and CNBC’s Halftime Report toasted their birthdays with special appearances. Burnett was surprised on set by her day-one guests, including John Avlon , Kevin Madden , and Bill Burton . Meanwhile, Halftime Report’s host Scott Wapner was joined by some of the show’s longest-serving committee members, including Josh Brown , Stephanie Link , Joe Terranova , and Steven Weiss , with others appearing throughout the program.

We're celebrating 15 years of Erin Burnett OutFront!

The OutFront team surprised Erin with a visit from some old friends of the show. pic.twitter.com/e2wsmIFLLy

— Erin Burnett OutFront (@OutFrontCNN) October 3, 2026

Revenue initiative : After seeing a reduction in federal funding, PBS News is joining the subscription bandwagon to generate additional revenue by launching Press Pass. The outlet says subscribers who contribute $8 per month or $96 per year to the program will “receive a new political newsletter, Inside the White House with Liz Landers , as well as interruption-free podcasts and select virtual events.”

Revolving Door: BBC News has found its new leader. Rachel Jupp was named director BBC News and Current Affairs. Jupp, currently director, BBC News documentaries and long-form journalism, was one of four finalists vying for this top position. She begins her new role in November.

“Rachel is an outstanding editorial leader, widely regarded for her news judgment, fairness, and high standards,” said Matt Brittin , BBC director-general. “She brings a clarity of vision for the future, and the determined, collaborative approach needed to strengthen BBC News.”

BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news https://t.co/Lle1w2E2mL

— BBC News (UK) (@BBCNews) October 5, 2026

Rob Schmitt has received a new multi-year deal from Newsmax. The host of the weeknight 7 p.m. ET show Rob Schmitt Tonight leads one of the network’s top-rated programs and, according to Gary Kanofsky , vp of news and programming, is responsible for growing Newsmax’s audience during that hour.

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Health Marketing Is Moving From Information to Navigation
articles.fullContent:
By Ashley Cisneros Mejia This post was created in partnership with Publicis Health

Healthcare no longer begins at a doctor’s office, and marketers need to adjust to that reality.

Marketers should consider how to empower patients and help them understand the vast amount of data at their fingertips.

Health marketers now need to consider how AI plays into the patient journey.

A health journey can now begin long before a formal moment of care, sparked by a smartwatch vibration, a TikTok scroll, or a question typed into an AI chatbot. The shift gives consumers more ways to engage with their health, and marketers many more signals to interpret.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ group chat co-hosted with Publicis Health, healthcare leaders discussed how AI, data, creativity, and culture are reshaping the patient experience.

The conversation opened with a simple question: Where did each speaker recently turn for health advice? Their answers reflected a journey that now flows among devices, platforms, personal networks, and clinical settings.

The range of responses underscored how far health influence has moved beyond the doctor’s office. Peter Scherr, CMO of Noom, shared that his father’s Apple Watch detected a heart anomaly, prompting him to seek care that eventually led to a pacemaker. “He consulted the device before his doctor,” Scherr said. “It drove home the point that health is everywhere.”

Matt McNally, global CEO of Publicis Health, said the industry is building on the long-running focus on the empowered patient. People have more information and tools than ever, but the journey has become more complex and continuous. “With the tools we have now, it’s our job to help people navigate the healthcare journey,” McNally noted.

The need for guidance is becoming more urgent as health data multiplies. Scherr pointed to the tension created by wearables, apps, blood work, and other inputs. “There’s a lot of data masquerading as answers,” he said. “It’s very overwhelming.”

For health brands, showing up across the journey requires more than visibility. Katie Baldwin, VP, consumer marketing at AbbVie, said pharma brands need to account for what consumers experience before, during, and after treatment, from the emotional reality of living with a condition to barriers that can shape whether someone starts or stays on therapy.

Baldwin framed the challenge facing marketers and agency partners as a dual responsibility. “Do you move them or do you arm them?” she remarked. “Moving them emotionally is what we trust our advertising agencies to do, and arming them with information is now just as critical.”

Equipping consumers with trustworthy information has become more challenging as AI tools become part of the health journey. Fannie McWatt, PhD, head of data and AI strategy at Publicis Health, said brands need to think beyond simply being findable in AI-powered search environments.

“Everybody’s talking about AEO and GEO, but for us, it’s more than optimization,” McWatt explained. “It’s actually looking at where AI is an influencer throughout the entire journey and what information in that particular situation needs to be retrieved at that moment.”

McWatt also cautioned that confidence and accuracy are not always the same thing. “We have to be really careful when we’re building the AI algorithms and structuring evidence and providing the context around it,” she continued.

As health decisions move across platforms, communities, creators, AI tools, and everyday conversations, brands have more opportunities to be useful in the places consumers already look for information.

Allison Ceraso, chief creative officer at Digitas Health, said health marketing has entered a more visible era. “Health isn’t in culture,” she said. “I think right now health is our culture. They are synonymous.”

The broader role demands more relevance, credible resources, and emotional intelligence. Ceraso explained that the best health brands start by understanding the fears, questions, and private moments that shape how people make sense of their health.

Craig Romanok, chief commercial officer at Digitas Health/Publicis Health, emphasized the scale of change facing the industry. “There’s no doubt we are at a moment right now, an inflection point in this category, this industry, that we have never seen before,” he said.

The group also discussed how connected data can help brands deliver more relevant support without crossing into intrusive territory. McNally predicted the next phase of patient support will depend on whether brands can anticipate the next point of friction.

“It’s not enough just to know me. That’s table stakes,” he said. “What do I need next? What am I going to need two weeks from now if I have a side effect that someone else on the product didn’t have?”

In health, relevance can build trust or erode it quickly. A consumer may want direction, but not surveillance. The opportunity is to show up with the right context at the right moment, then make the decision point easier to navigate.

For Ceraso, that responsibility is what makes health marketing different. “People don’t want your product all the time; they need it,” she said. “So, you have to come into the conversation with empathy and understanding.”

As health becomes more predictive and proactive, technology will only carry the work so far. The true test is whether brands can make critical moments feel clearer, better timed, and more human.

articles.title: Brands Can Expect a Longer Holiday Shopping Season and Thriftier Consumers
articles.fullContent:
By Dawn Papandrea This post was created in partnership with Ibotta

Elevated grocery prices and anticipated holiday financial stress are already making shoppers more selective   about which brands earn a spot in their carts.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ panel co-hosted with Ibotta, Ryan Joe, editor-in-chief of ADWEEK, sat down with Chris Dungan, VP of client partnerships at Ibotta, and Krystle Rocci, integrated strategy director of Pernod Ricard, to discuss how data-driven media spend can help brands adapt to changing shopping behaviors and connect with consumers in the moments that matter.

The chat kicked off with a discussion on how Ibotta first-party data is helping Pernod Ricard, which owns a portfolio of spirit brands, measure the success of its promotions.

When Pernod considers how to move large volumes of product quickly, a promotion is often the mechanism to do that, Dungan explained. With Ibotta’s first-party data, Pernod can identify and attribute what changed consumers’ buying behavior during the promotion. “It allows you to better measure and attribute the success of the campaign,” he said.

Rocci noted the importance of looking beyond impression count to make sure your ad resonates.

“Are they seeing an ad in the right moment, in the right mindset, to get them to perform an intended action, and is it driving them down that purchase funnel through the journey? It’s really about hitting them in the moments that matter, which for spirits, is super important,” she explained.

The conversation shifted to how Ibotta and Pernod are adapting to changing shopping trends for this holiday season. Consumers this year are shopping earlier instead of condensing all their purchasing into the couple of weeks before the holiday.

“Consumers are elongating that purchasing period. They’re trying to flatten that consumption curve,” said Dungan.

The key is figuring out how to intercept consumers within that decision path. “The timing is getting earlier and earlier, so how can we get in their mind before they’re at the shelf or at the cart, so that when they do actually make the decision, they’re choosing one of our products,” said Rocci.

Promotions are a good tool for attracting first-time or lapsed buyers, but getting the consumer to choose the brand the next time they buy the category is the true loyalty test, Dungan shared.

That’s where the brand works to create a relationship with the customer, added Rocci. “Whether that is the bottle or the flavor profile or the price point or the continued re-engaging content to give them meaning around that brand, I think that’s all helpful,” she said.

In addition to repeat purchases, Pernod wants to encourage buyers to explore the full brand portfolio. “Sometimes our brands can complement one another. For example, Absolut and Kahlua partner together on the espresso martini,” said Rocci.

Dungan and Rocci pointed out the benefits of individual brand leaders working together for the good of the organization.

“If we can ultimately think about growing baskets and collective equity for the organization, making consumers buy more products overall, it benefits that organization meaningfully,” said Dungan.

Leveraging promotions, scaling purchases across multiple products, and driving greater incremental sales over a tight period of time is the kind of “messaging that lands with CFOs as well as CMOs,” Dungan concluded.

articles.title: People Are Getting Together—Will Brands Meet Up With Them?
articles.fullContent:
By Justin Chin This post was created in partnership with Atmosphere TV

Consumers are forgoing solitary time for social experiences, spending time in public spaces like bars, gyms, and restaurants. This shift presents a unique opportunity for brands that are ready to capitalize on this shared attention.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ panel co-hosted with Atmosphere TV, Zoë Ruderman, chief content officer at ADWEEK, sat down with Blake Sabatinelli, CEO of Atmosphere TV, and Lindsay Sutton, SVP and head of marketing for Atmosphere TV, to discuss how brands can enter communal spaces and make an authentic impact on audiences.

Sabatinelli opened the conversation by pointing to the post-pandemic cultural shift in leisure time and how people are more thoughtful about who they spend their time with and what they spend their time doing.

Community experiences matter again, he said, giving brands new opportunities to reach people “at the right time, the right place, with the right message in a way that’s far less disrupted and more accepted than what you get in other formats.”

Sabatinelli added that these communal spaces don’t just offer brands large audiences but also the heightened emotions of real-time connection.

“If you think about the mindset and mentality that you’re in when you’re watching sports, just think about the energy and the feeling that you have,” Sabatinelli said. “And if you’re a brand, you want to be associated with that feeling and that energy because it’s bringing a positive mindset.”

Sutton explained that there are nuances in marketing in these spaces. Brands should avoid producing campaigns that feel intrusive or distracting to the experience, a process Sutton’s team at Atmosphere TV helps guide.

She added that it’s a collaboration between brands and her team: “We will ask, ‘What makes sense for this moment?’ and build that together.”

Sabatinelli shared that brands that have worked with Atmosphere TV in the past have had to think “out of the box.” He shared a story about a campaign for a financial services partner that had an interactive ad that tracked runners during the Boston Marathon.

“We’re doing things that you can’t get anywhere else because we have an engineering team that sits down and works with brands,” he said.

Sutton has a unique perspective of being a creative brand strategist before joining Atmosphere TV, and candidly shared that she and her team originally “weren’t thinking about the communal space as a place that we could tap, that you could get additional value out of.” She admitted the default channels were traditional platforms that were “tried and true.”

“We always thought about marketing as one person traveling along their journey, vs. these much larger moments or shared moments that we could have been planning for,” Sutton said.

Sabatinelli offered some advice for brand marketers who may be shy about getting into this new market.

“Marketers need to think about the media ecosystems that exist outside of Meta and Google. We’ve reached a point of saturation on those platforms, especially when it comes to acquisition,” Sabatinelli said. “At a certain point, you’re going to have to find another modality to reach people.”

Justin Chin is a contributing writer for ADWEEK.

articles.title: Building the Right Team Is More Important Than Ever for Marketers
articles.fullContent:
By Justin Chin This post was created in partnership with Weber Shandwick

As AI streamlines workflows and marketing budgets tighten, human collaboration and partnership remain as important as ever to create strong creative.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ Marketing Vanguard roundtable panel co-hosted by Weber Shandwick, Jenny Rooney, chief brand and community officer at ADWEEK, and Karen Pugliese, CEO of Weber Shandwick, gathered with C-suite executives to discuss how brands can put together the right marketing team with a mix of both in-house staff and agency partners.

Pugliese shared the stage with marketing and growth executives from three Weber Shandwick clients—Unilever, Supergoop!, and PurposeBuilt Brands. She views Weber Shandwick’s role with clients like these as a partner, not a vendor, and prefers to start working with brands as early in the creative process as possible.

“We want to get into it with brands when the clay is still wet. Because that’s how we make the work better together,” Pugliese shared. “That’s what collaboration looks like; how we get to great work.”

Jon Bellante, CMO of PurposeBuilt Brands, added that two of his company’s brands brought on Weber Shandwick for that close collaboration.

“We ultimately wanted to move faster and, essentially, get rid of the agency reveal,” Bellante said. “We needed to have a partner that was going to be an extension of our team that we could collaborate with on an ongoing basis.”

Lauren Weinberg, CMO of Supergoop! is working with a new team, which has pushed her to work collaboratively and quickly. She likes being “in the work” and doesn’t worry about hierarchy among her staff.

“Whenever we review work in a group setting, I always go last because I want to make sure everyone else’s voice is heard before I say whatever I’m going to say,” Weinberg explained. “I think bringing those divergent perspectives to the table and having us debate it openly allows us to move quickly and helps us create the best work.”

For Melanie Cappella, chief growth officer of cooking aids and mini meals at Unilever Foods U.S., working with her team early is important. In the past, she’s found it hard to make changes once a project or campaign is close to being finished.

“Being involved in the early phases and making sure that you see the brief, you see the assignment that’s going over to the agency partners, and that you are in the first early rounds of shaping an idea, can really leave an impact,” Cappella said.

When Weinberg built her team at Supergoop!, she looked for employees who could adapt and were willing to experiment with new AI tools.

Looking ahead, as AI streamlines workflows, Weinberg seeks out candidates with qualities in the “humanity space,” like creativity, communication, and being in touch with culture.

“It’s those kinds of skills combined with the right mindset and the ability to be agile that I think are most important in a world where you can have AI take on different tasks,” Weinberg added.

Justin Chin is a contributing writer for ADWEEK.

articles.title: Award-Winning Agencies Talk TikTok
articles.fullContent:
By Dawn Papandrea This post was created in partnership with TikTok for Business

Media buying should be more than placing ads—it should help brands connect with audiences, navigate a changing media landscape, and make every investment count. Done well, it turns attention into action and helps shape how brands grow.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ panel co-hosted with TikTok, Alexia Nüssli, head of product strategy and operations for TikTok, invited representatives from two agency winners in the inaugural TikTok Media Buying Excellence Awards to discuss how their TikTok-first strategies are driving outsized impact for their clients.

The TikTok Media Buying Excellence Awards recognize independent agency partners setting new standards in media buying through innovation, measurable business impact, and a commitment to helping brands succeed on TikTok.

Highlighting that commitment, Nüssli opened the panel by explaining how TikTok operates as a fast-evolving platform for brands to drive both cultural relevance and measurable media outcomes, and how independent agencies play an important role in making that happen.

“Brands turn to agencies not just for media performance; they turn to agencies to drive holistic business growth,” Nüssli said.

She then welcomed Zayit Bemmel, associate director of paid advertising, fashion for Power Digital, and Warren Jolly, co-founder and CEO of Adquadrant, to share some of their media-buying insights.

Bemmel shared how her agency uses TikTok’s advanced measurement testing tools to lean into incrementality. “We’re constantly ensuring that within our media mix models, with all of our clients, whether it’s fashion or CPG, that we’re pressure testing what we’re running on TikTok,” she explained. Rigorous testing helps Bemmel’s team determine when to increase or pull back on spend.

Next, Jolly spoke about his agency’s use of TikTok to leverage AI content. “I think there’s a lot that we can learn in the U.S. from what’s happening in APAC, and one component of that is AI content,” he asserted. “Even if you’re a brand that’s very anti-AI creative or conscious about it, leveraging AI-generated content as a construct to test narratives and to build at scale and meet the demands of the creative supply chain is a great opportunity for differentiation.”

Both agency leaders alluded to the breakneck pace at which TikTok introduces innovative new tools, and the incredible opportunity that gives to agile agencies and their clients.

“Part of the value that agencies can bring to brands is just keeping them at the cutting edge of an organization that’s evolving, shipping new product very fast, and is clearly a disruptor,” said Jolly.

Nüssli invited the panelists to share some advice on how to maximize their TikTok strategies. Bemmell encouraged brands to lean into the recommendations that TikTok and agency partners have.

“We are following their guidance in tandem with our best practices and expertise that we have across our entire team to lean into things like TikTok Shop or the new tools that they have,” Bemmel explained. “Once your clients trust you and you are that partner, they’re going to be way more bullish and willing to test into those tools.”

Jolly reinforced his belief about the need to stay relevant in the age of AI. “TikTok is probably the best partner to unpack what those opportunities look like and actually operationalize towards them,” he said.

articles.fullContent:
What does Instagram verification mean?

Instagram verification is the process of getting a blue checkmark badge that appears next to your username on the platform. The verification badge signals to other users on the platform that an account really belongs to the user, artist, brand, or organization it represents.

If you’re looking to enhance your presence while pursuing verification, consider brainstorming unique Instagram username ideas that reflect your brand identity.

Your favorite celebrity probably has a blue checkmark on their account:

Brands with a strong social media following usually have a verified badge too:

But there are actually two types of verification: traditional verification and paid.

Originally, verification was only available to “notable and unique” people or brands. The process of awarding that coveted blue checkmark was shrouded in mystery, and verification was usually restricted to celebrities and big brand names.

These days, users can also pay for verification through Meta Verified. That means anyone can get a verified badge on their Instagram or Facebook accounts.

Whichever route you take, the payoff is the same:

  • Legitimacy and trust: The verification process requires a government-issued ID, so having a verified badge establishes your account authenticity and helps the community know it’s the real you. People are more likely to follow, message, and do business with an account they can confirm is genuine.
  • Impersonation protection: Fake accounts exist for all kinds of reasons, from scams to parodies. A badge sets your account apart from impersonators, and Meta Verified adds proactive account monitoring to help protect your account from impersonators or hackers.
  • Visibility and performance: Verified accounts appear at or near the top of comments and search results when people type in a business name. They also appear as a recommended business to follow in the Feed, which can translate into more followers, website clicks, and conversions.
  • Extra features: Verified accounts get access to perks like exclusive stickers on Instagram Stories and Reels to help their content stand out.

No matter which method an account used to get verified, the blue checkmark looks the same. That means it’s impossible to know whether it was awarded to a user through traditional means or if they’re paying for the Meta Verified service.

Who can get verified on Instagram?

Anyone can request a verified badge on Instagram. Though the requirements are slightly different for each type of verification.

Traditional verification requirements

If you want to go through the traditional verification process for your Instagram profile, you can apply for the blue badge if you’re a notable public figure, celebrity, or brand, and you meet the eligibility criteria.

Instagram’s criteria is a bit vague, but here’s what we do know.

In addition to following Instagram’s Terms of Use and Community Guidelines, your account also needs to be:

  • Authentic: It must represent a real person, registered business, or entity.
  • Unique: Only one account per person or business may be verified, with exceptions for language-specific accounts. Instagram generally doesn’t verify general interest accounts.
  • Complete: Your account must be public and complete. That means you must have a bio, profile photo, and active account when applying.
  • Notable: Your account must represent a well-known, highly searched-for person, brand, or entity.

What counts as “notable” to one person may not be notable to another, which is why verification used to be out of reach for most Instagram users.

But don’t despair. There’s now another option: Subscribing to Meta Verified.

Meta Verified requirements

Getting a blue tick through Meta Verified is much more simple.

Here’s what you need to subscribe:

  • Be at least 18 years old
  • Be located in a country that offers Meta Verified
  • Have a public or private profile that’s associated with your full name, aligns with naming standards, and has a profile picture that includes your face
  • Meet minimum activity requirements, such as prior posting history
  • A government-issued ID or driver’s license
  • Two-factor authentication enabled on your profile
  • Follow Instagram’s Terms of Use and Community Guidelines

For brand teams, this is the results page showing their company’s name. Ahrefs’ panel also tracked where these AI Overviews appeared and the external sites they linked to. Ahrefs doesn’t report clicks on these queries or how often the brand’s website is cited in responses.

The 83% figure in Ahrefs’ headline comes from a broader set of U.S. desktop crawls conducted on Sept. 29, not from this panel. Additionally, two other counts from that week, by DemandSphere and Chris Long, used their own data samples.

On Sept. 30, Chris Long, co-founder of Nectiv, shared on LinkedIn that he “ran a quick scrape with SerpApi this morning and found that 93 out of 100 enterprise brands had AI Overviews present for them.” Long didn’t publish the full list of 100 brands.

DemandSphere’s daily series, published October 1 , tracked branded keywords using its DemandMetrics platform, which looks at their presence across “all markets, all devices” once a day. The data showed that AI Overviews appeared in 26.12% of those keywords on Sept. 1, then reached 90.48% on Sept. 27, before dropping to 82.06% on Sept. 29.

Before Sept. 26, the daily percentage was below 60%. DemandSphere defines an AI Overview as present “regardless of whether brand itself is cited in the AIO.”

Separately from its brand-name panel, Ahrefs analyzed 92.5 million branded-keyword crawls out of 232.8 million U.S. desktop crawls between July and September. Their monthly data showed that 61.3% of branded keywords triggered AI Overviews in July, rising to 65.1% in August, and reaching 73.3% in September, a 12-percentage-point increase, compared to a 4.8-point rise for non-branded keywords, which averaged 78.3% in September. On Sept. 29, AI Overviews appeared in 82.91% of U.S. desktop results for branded keywords.

Neither vendor explains its branded-keyword classification. DemandSphere does not give its keyword count. Ahrefs gives crawl counts for its broader analysis without stating how many distinct keywords they represent. Each crawl is a results page collected by the company, not a specific user search.

Ahrefs selected the panel’s brands from Interbrand’s Best Global Brands 2025 and searched each brand’s name alone. They describe this set as “a separate sample” from their broader analysis, focusing specifically on brand names rather than every search that includes a brand. Ahrefs’ post doesn’t explain why two of the July 1 results couldn’t be used.

The weekly counts are illustrated in a chart within the post, showing U.S. results and crediting Ahrefs Keywords Explorer as the source. Device and detailed collection settings are not stated.

The labeled counts are five on July 1, 13 on July 29, and again 13 on Aug. 26. At the checkpoint before Sept. 9, the count was 16, then it jumped to 42 on that date. By the checkpoint before Sept. 30, it increased again to 46 and reached 63 on Sept. 30. Ahrefs mentioned that AI Overviews “vastly increased at the start of September.”

On Sept. 30, they also recorded the position of each of the 63 AI Overviews on the page. Of these, 48 appeared in what Ahrefs calls position one, eight in position two, two in position three, three in position four, and two in position six, with none in position five.

The average position was 1.49 for all 63, and the median was one. The post does not define position. Ahrefs suggests Google could “move these AI Overviews lower in the SERP”; however, from the placement counts it is unclear whether a brand’s own listing moved down the page.

Chris Long’s Sept. 30 post said “competitors/external sources can now control the narrative of your brand directly in the search results.” In its separate 100-brand panel, Ahrefs recorded which outside sites the brand-name answers cited.

For AI Overviews collected from Sept. 16 to 29, Ahrefs had source lists for 57 and counted how many of those cited each outside domain. It describes those external citations as links from “websites other than the brand queried.”

Which outside sites the brand-name answers cited

Of 57 AI Overviews with source lists in Ahrefs’ U.S. brand-name panel. Counts are answers citing each domain.

Walmart 4 of 57 7.0% SEARCH Brand name AI Overview Sources Editorial illustration · not an actual search result

One AI Overview can cite more than one domain.

A cited platform may host pages managed by the brand. These domain counts don’t identify page ownership.

Bar lengths use a common 0–100% scale. Shares are not additive.

Source: Ahrefs SERP crawls: Sept. 16–29, 2026.

Out of 57 source lists, the company identified just one verified competitor-owned website. Among the 58 responses where the full text was accessible, two (or 3.4%) directly discussed competitors. For example, Pepsi’s answer referenced Coca-Cola when talking about the “cola wars,” while Intel’s response mentioned TSMC and Nvidia.

Platforms like YouTube and LinkedIn allow brands to run channels and manage company pages. However, Ahrefs’ post doesn’t specify how many of the cited pages belong to the brands themselves.

These citation counts show how many answers cited each listed domain, but they don’t tell us who influenced the wording or whether the information shared was accurate.

The Ahrefs panel reviewed the results page for each brand’s exact name. One suggested check for brand and SEO leaders is to search their company’s precise name on Google and review the AI Overview and the referenced pages.

Each search provides a snapshot at a specific moment. Repeating the check on different days gives you dated snapshots of what Google shows for your name.

Agencies reporting branded performance can use Search Console’s branded queries filter , which Google announced in November 2025 and opened to all eligible sites in March. It shows clicks, impressions, average position, and click-through rate for queries Google classifies as branded. Google sorts queries with an AI-assisted system that can count typos as branded, along with queries for a unique product or service that don’t use the brand name. Roger Montti covered Google’s answers about the filter in March.

The filter is limited to top-level properties with “a sufficient volume of queries and impressions,” and its definition of branded is Google’s, separate from either vendor’s. In Montti’s report, Google’s John Mueller said there was no way to add queries to the filter “at the moment” and that he wasn’t “aware of plans to provide customization.” By that account, there was no way in March to edit the filter’s branded set to match a vendor’s keyword list.

A change in branded clicks alone doesn’t indicate whether brand demand has changed or if an AI Overview was involved. Late September also isn’t a confirmed rollout date.

Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

These signals are easy to miss when you rely on alerts alone because each one can seem too minor to warrant attention. With social intelligence, Atlas Copco Group brings those signals together to spot patterns that need a closer look before they impact business performance.

Atlas Copco Group’s 5-step reputation intelligence model

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

The model is based on five practices that help them spot emerging risk, strengthen brand presence and manage issues consistently.

1. Catch weak signals early

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

To identify which weak signals matter for your brand, start with the reputation risks you already monitor and work backward. What behaviors, questions or changes tend to show up before those risks become more serious? Those early indicators can become the signals your team tracks more closely.

Using Sprout Social Listening, the Atlas team tracks these patterns across channels and spots connections that might be easy to miss when looking at each account on its own. From there, the team can then investigate what’s happening and decide whether a local market needs more guidance.

2. Establish a clear governance framework

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Those shared expectations also strengthen brand safety. When multiple teams and contributors manage social accounts, clear ownership and review processes create more consistency around how teams publish content and respond to potential issues.

Atlas Copco Group uses Tagging in Sprout to organize content by quality and compliance, track which teams are meeting brand standards and identify where additional support is needed.

3. Standardize account health metrics

Atlas Copco Group uses a consistent set of metrics to evaluate brand health in various markets. The team looks at activity, brand compliance, response times and audience engagement together to create a more objective view of performance.

articles.title: How to use social listening and media monitoring for corporate reputation management
articles.fullContent:
You spend years managing a vibrant, positive brand reputation—nailing the customer experience, delivering great service and watching your reputation thrive. But all it takes is one viral post to make that hard work feel like it’s disappearing overnight.

Even the most experienced marketers face this reality. According to an Axios Harris Poll, 46% of corporate reputations have declined between 2019 and 2025.

Managing brand sentiment can feel overwhelming, but you can take control of your brand’s narrative with a smart corporate reputation management strategy.

What is corporate reputation management?

Corporate reputation management is the practice of proactively influencing and maintaining how the public perceives your brand. This includes monitoring conversations about your company, resolving issues quickly and amplifying positive moments to shape your brand perception.

Corporate reputation management and online reputation management go hand-in-hand. For modern brands, the key aspect that sets them apart is the online focus, which highlights how digital conversations unfolding online shape brand perception and how customers expect you to actively listen on social.

According to a Q2 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey, consumers say social is the number one place they hear about a brand crisis first. And when a crisis happens, 64% of consumers say it’s important for a brand to respond publicly on social media rather than through a press release or website statement. This is why social media teams are on the front lines, tasked with protecting and nurturing brand reputation.

A great example of managing a ‘crisis’ online—and getting ahead of the conversation— is the 2018 #ChickenCrises. When KFC ran out of chicken and had to shut down over 750 stores, customers were not happy. Using social listening, the brand noticed the backlash brewing online and quickly addressed the issue with an edgy, self-aware response. They rearranged the letters “KFC” on a chicken bucket to look like a curse word, essentially saying: “We messed up.”

This light-hearted, authentic response defused tension, protected the brand’s reputation and sparked viral trends. And there’s a reason we’re still talking about it eight years later: it’s become an iconic example of a brand apology. It reinforces how vital it is for social media professionals to listen, engage and collaborate with stakeholders to manage reputation challenges to shape brand perception.

Trust impacts everyone from consumers to investors (63% cite it as a critical factor in business-related decisions, according to the Phillips Group). As a marketing leader, your opportunity is to proactively build and protect corporate reputation by engaging with audience conversations and influencing your company’s narrative, wherever it happens.

Why corporate reputation management is important today

Your reputation shapes every part of your business, from winning stakeholder trust to driving sales and building customer loyalty. Because reputation is foundational to brand health, damage to it is one of the biggest risks companies face today.

In highly regulated sectors like financial services, social media acts as an early warning system; a single misunderstood fee structure or service outage can escalate into a compliance nightmare if not addressed with immediate, transparent communication.

The classic Harvard Business Review’s Reputation and Its Risks, notes that 70-80% of the modern economy’s market value comes from “hard-to-assess intangible assets,” like brand equity. This means anything that can hinder your brand—a bad reputation, a crisis—has the power to affect your entire business. Modern data confirms this: Aon’s findings rank reputation damage as the eighth biggest risk to companies worldwide.

But even when you do everything right, outside factors may still influence your reputation. In 2025, a user on Reddit reported that GameStop had charged customers for unreceived products following a $1.4 million merchandise heist.

Rather than letting the issue escalate, GameStop’s social media team acted quickly with a proactive response that clarified that no customer orders were affected. This action helped the company protect its reputation and maintain brand trust.

Source: Reddit

GameStop’s social media response made the difference between protecting its reputation and letting a false story spread unchecked. Their social team listened, researched the facts and responded quickly with clarity.

By spotting issues early and responding quickly, your company reduces the impact of negative reputation events. But reputation management is more than avoiding the negative. As a marketer, you also have the ability to proactively nurture your brand perception online to get ahead of risk, too.

Take Atlas Copco group as an example. The organization uses social listening and intelligence to identify sentiment and trends online, and to address small issues before they become brand risks. The team saw that many risks don’t start as large spikes. They show up first as small, repeatable instances like questions, inconsistencies in activity or brand content, and even how local markets experience the brand differently. Each little concern doesn’t seem alarming, but when stacked together, the brand risks start to become clear.

Understanding these patterns through regular listening led them to use social data to push for increased training and governance for internal teams, so they could address inconsistencies early and act before the small moments escalated into larger reputation concerns.

  1. Data storytelling combines three pillars (data, narrative, and visuals) to turn numbers into compelling, shareable content.

What is data storytelling?

Data storytelling is the practice of using facts, statistics, and quantitative information to build a compelling narrative that an audience can understand and act on. In other words, it uses real numbers to support an engaging story and authenticate the story’s message.

“Using data to tell stories from a brand’s point of view can be very effective, as it bridges that place between logic and emotion and lets a brand connect with a reader on a deeper level,” says Leeann Froese, Digital Marketing Manager at Town Hall Brands.

Data can “prove” the validity of a story (for example, sheep are smart: Research shows they can remember the visual identities of up to 50 individual faces) and help sell a brand or product (Ie: When “four out of five dentists” recommend a specific toothpaste).

That brings us to another important part of data storytelling: the numbers need to be true, unaltered, and preferably provided by a trusted third party. Making up numbers or bending statistics to suit your own needs is a dangerous game, especially on social media.

Every good data story rests on three things working together: the data itself, the narrative around it, and the visuals that carry it.

What are the three pillars of data storytelling?

The three pillars of data storytelling are data, narrative, and visualization. Drop any one of them and the story falls flat: data alone is dry, narrative alone is unproven, and visuals alone are decoration.

Data

The foundation is accurate, relevant, and verifiable information. That might be third-party research, platform data, or your own first-party numbers from sales, surveys, or social analytics.

Whatever the origin, it needs to come from trusted sources you can name publicly. If you cannot point to where a number came from, it does not belong in the story.

Narrative

Narrative is what gives the numbers meaning. It supplies the context (why this matters now), the stakes (who is affected), and the takeaway (what the audience should do next).

A 12% increase is just arithmetic until you explain what changed and who it changed things for. That framing is what moves a stat from forgettable to shareable.

Visualization

Visuals make data accessible and memorable in a feed built for speed. “The brain processes visual information much faster than text,” says Froese.

The format should match the message. Single-stat graphics work for one big number, bar charts for comparisons, line charts for change over time, and carousels when the story needs a few beats to land.

What are the 5 C’s of storytelling?

The 5 C’s of storytelling are Context, Characters, Conflict, Climax, and Closure. It is a classic narrative arc, and it maps neatly onto data storytelling when you treat your audience as the characters and your insight as the climax.

Used together, the 5 C’s keep a data post from becoming a list of figures. They give the numbers a beginning, a middle, and a reason to care.

Data storytelling matters because it gives social content a layer of proof that most posts lack, and proof is what builds brand authority at scale. Social media might not be “real life,” but what we post (especially from a business perspective) has real-life consequences. As technology progresses and social platforms grow, information spreads quickly, and 79% of adults globally say social media has made people easier to manipulate with false information.

When you use data storytelling in social media, you’re arming your content with an extra layer of validity. By offering proof, sharing statistics and being transparent about numbers, you can set your brand apart from the rest.

articles.title: ChatGPT Gets GPT-6 And Intelligent UI For Interactive Answers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 in ChatGPT worldwide, introducing the new Intelligent UI that combines text, visuals, and interactive features. The update is rolling out beginning today in the Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, and will extend to Free and Go users from tomorrow.

In Chat, GPT-6 operates on GPT-6 Sol for the plans included in today’s rollout and on GPT-6 Luna for Free and Go. Enterprise access varies based on admin configurations, and the models supporting ChatGPT Work and Codex stay unchanged with this update.

The company’s help page explains that GPT-6 replaces the ‘Latest’ option in the model menu, while GPT-5.6 Sol stays available as a separate option. The Intelligent UI feature is gradually being introduced on the web and supported, updated apps, at thinking levels from Instant to Extra High. The Pro thinking level continues to run on GPT-6 Astra but doesn’t support this feature, and neither do the older ChatGPT desktop apps for macOS and Windows.

Sol and Luna launched on Sept. 22 for ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API, when the company said they weren’t yet available in Chat.

OpenAI says it trained GPT-6 to decide how each response is laid out based on the question. Responses can include buttons, forms, and charts, and ChatGPT can still answer in plain text when that’s the most useful format.

The announcement describes the tool-building this way:

“You can also ask ChatGPT to create a tool for the task at hand, such as a calculator to explore how savings could grow, a bill splitter for dinner with friends, or a game you can play in the conversation.”

ChatGPT already offered interactive charts, added in June, and interactive modules for more than 70 math and science topics, added in March, according to its release notes .

If you prefer fewer visuals, you can turn off the Layout and visuals setting on the web. Keep in mind, though, that some visual elements might still show up, as mentioned on the help page.

GPT-6 can begin providing answers even while it’s still thinking or working with tools, and then share more insights without waiting for the user to ask again.

For questions that need web search, the company says GPT-6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant.

It also says GPT-6 makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer. In an internal test of difficult problems, it reports that GPT-6 addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT-5.6, without giving a figure.

Two of OpenAI’s tool examples, a savings calculator and bill splitter, use generic inputs and public math. In August, I observed that these tools are the easiest for Google’s generative UI to replicate as it began appearing in AI Overviews. Calculator and converter pages might also be challenged by ChatGPT-created tools, which enable users to request and utilize them directly in the chat, eliminating the need to leave the conversation.

OpenAI aims for ChatGPT to gradually create more of the user interfaces needed for daily tasks.

Today’s GPT-6 announcement doesn’t say how sources will appear when responses are presented as charts, comparisons, or tools. As mentioned on ChatGPT’s search help page , answers that incorporate web search results might include citations, which can be accessed via a Sources button whenever it’s available.

articles.title: How to build brand loyalty: 7 strategies that work for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand loyalty is the emotional connection that drives customers to repeatedly choose one brand over alternatives, even when cheaper or more convenient options exist.
  2. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others.
  3. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs.
  4. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis.

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible.

The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action.

What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale.

[contentuprade]

Brand loyalty vs. customer loyalty

Brand loyalty and customer loyalty sound interchangeable, but they come from different places. Brand loyalty is emotional and identity-driven. Customer loyalty is usually transactional, powered by price, points, or convenience. Both are worth having, but only one survives a competitor’s discount.

The brand loyalty pyramid

The brand loyalty pyramid was developed in the 1990s by David Aaker, hailed as “the father of modern branding.”

Just as the sales funnel shows how potential buyers move through the conversion process, the brand loyalty pyramid shows how customers move through the process to becoming brand-loyal.

The pyramid has five stages:

  • Switchers: People who have bought your product but are just as likely to buy a competitor’s product next time.
  • Habitual buyers: People who buy your products out of habit but could easily be swayed to another product if it’s cheaper or more convenient.
  • Satisfied buyers with switching costs: People who are satisfied with your brand but primarily stick with your products because there are barriers to switching (such as learning how to use a new tool or platform, or having to buy new cords or accessories).
  • Buyers who like the brand: At this point the connection becomes emotional, and the buyer becomes passionate about your brand for reasons they may not be able to articulate clearly.
  • Committed buyers: These are the people lining up to buy a new product the moment it launches. They love your brand and aren’t afraid to show it.

Source: Aaker, D.A. (1991) Managing Brand Equity. The Free Press, New York.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty matters because it lowers what you spend to grow and raises what each customer is worth. It’s obvious that you want people to choose your brand over your competitors. Brand loyalty ensures they do so again and again. But it provides more value to your brand than the simple revenue from customer retention and each purchase. Here’s why.

How loyal customers reduce acquisition costs and increase lifetime value

Acquiring a new customer is harder (and more expensive) than selling to a repeat customer.

Part of that is targeting efficiency. The more interaction you have with a customer or prospect, the better you can personalize your offers. Plus, you can target specific conversion goals (upsell? refill?) rather than using CPM awareness marketing campaigns.

Loyalty also cushions you when budgets tighten. When consumers cut back, the brands they already trust are the ones they keep buying, which makes retained revenue more predictable than new-customer revenue during uncertain periods.

Brand loyalty increases your lifetime customer value. That, in turn, increases the amount that you can afford to spend on customer acquisition and increases the ROI of your social marketing strategy.

Why loyal customers drive word of mouth and advocacy

Loyal customers do more than buy your products themselves. They share their love for your product with others, which turns retention into a growth channel. That value shows up in written customer feedback and in everyday word of mouth.

Word of mouth is the most common source of brand discovery among internet users in the United States. And shared social content (the digital version of word of mouth) is the most powerful way to turn brand awareness into consideration.

What drives brand loyalty?

Loyalty isn’t one big gesture. It’s the accumulation of small, repeated signals that a brand is reliable and worth caring about. Researchers

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.

Key takeaways

  1. Engagement rate measures how many people interact with your social content relative to reach, impressions, or follower count. It includes actions like likes, comments, shares, and saves, but not passive views.

  3. A good engagement rate typically falls between 1% and 5%, but benchmarks vary significantly by platform and industry. Always compare against your specific platform and industry, not a universal standard.
  4. Tracking engagement rate over time shows which content resonates, which formats to prioritize, and where to adjust your strategy. Perch by Hootsuite automates that tracking across all your accounts, and social media analytics tools can also provide industry benchmarks for comparison.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is a social media metric that measures how much of your audience actively engages with your content. It defines the amount of interaction a piece of content (or a campaign, or a whole account) gets compared to reach or audience size.

Engagement metrics vary by channel, but in general, it’s any action someone takes to interact with your content, including likes, comments, shares, saves, poll responses, messages, or link clicks. Because each platform counts engagement a little differently, it helps to know exactly what actions feed into your social media engagement rate before you calculate it.

Engagement rate matters because it shows whether your content is actually connecting with your audience. When people take the time to like, comment, share, or save a post, it’s a strong signal that they find it interesting or useful.

Second, higher engagement rates help you get better visibility on social media platforms. That’s because social algorithms surface more engaging content to new audiences.

A lot of engagement on your content also makes you look more trustworthy and appealing to first-time profile visitors, especially if there’s an active conversation happening in your comments. For enterprise teams, engagement rate is also one of the clearest ways to prove social ROI to leadership, since it ties content performance to real audience behavior.

What counts as engagement on each platform?

Engagement is any action a user takes to interact with your content, but the specific actions that count vary from platform to platform. Knowing what feeds into the formula helps you calculate an accurate engagement rate and compare performance fairly across channels.

Here’s what typically counts as engagement on each major social network:

  • Instagram: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and replies to Stories.
  • TikTok: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and follows generated by a video.
  • Facebook: Reactions, comments, shares, and clicks on links or buttons.
  • LinkedIn: Reactions, comments, shares (reposts), and clicks.
  • X (Twitter): Likes, replies, reposts, quote posts, and clicks.
  • Pinterest: Saves (repins), comments, clicks, and close-ups.

Passive metrics like impressions and views usually don’t count as engagement on their own, since they measure exposure rather than interaction. When in doubt, check the platform’s analytics to confirm which actions it includes before running your numbers.

How to calculate engagement rate (6 formulas)

The standard engagement rate formula is total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. That said, there are six variations worth knowing, because each one uses a different denominator and answers a slightly different question.

  1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common.
  2. Engagement rate by post (ER post): Best for specific posts.
  3. Engagement rate by impressions (ER impressions): Best for paid content.
  4. Daily engagement rate (Daily ER): Best for long-term analysis.
  5. Engagement rate by views (ER views): Best for video.
  6. Cost per engagement (CPE): Best for influencer marketing or conversion-based campaigns.

1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common

This is the most common engagement rate formula. ERR measures the percentage of people who interact with your content after seeing it.

Here’s how to calculate engagement rate for a single post:

ERR = total number of engagements on a post / reach of that post * 100

To calculate the average ERR across multiple posts, add together the ERR for each post and divide by the total number of posts:

Average ERR = Total ERR / Number of posts

For example: Post 1 (3.4%) + Post 2 (3.5%) / 2 = 3.45%

Pros: Because not all followers see every post, ERR is often more accurate than follower-based metrics, especially in algorithm-driven feeds. Reach includes both followers and non-followers who discover content through search, shares, hashtags, and recommendations.

Cons: Reach can fluctuate for a variety of reasons, making it a difficult variable to control. ...
